clue.text: Holiday destination reserved, but no time

indicators.note: 'no time' asks for the abbreviation for time to be dropped from the phrase before it

blocks.note: kept back for later use, as a two-word phrase
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A holiday spot has been booked, but there's no time to go.
explanation.walkthrough: SET ASIDE loses its T to leave SEASIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: The coast is the classic British place to spend a summer break, so it is a typical holiday spot.

clue.text: Dry hill zone

blocks.note: sec is the French word used on wine labels for dry
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a description of arid upland; dry and hill are separate pieces, and only the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector is a distinct area or district marked off from others, much as a zone is.

clue.text: Fly, one trapped in a barrel, right wing in ale

indicators.note: something trapped in a barrel sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the right wing of a word is its rightmost edge, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a vat is a large barrel or tub for liquids
the Roman numeral for one
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fly has fallen into a barrel of beer and is stuck there.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside A VAT to make AVIAT, then the last letter of ale finishes AVIATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To aviate is to pilot an aircraft, a formal verb for flying.

clue.text: Without offering protection, bank going after us, nice when bankrupt!

indicators.note: a business gone bankrupt is broken up, so these letters are broken and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
to bank on someone is to rely on them

explanation.surface: A bank fails its customers, leaving them unprotected, after going under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going after' places the bank word after the rearranged letters. Bank here is a verb, as in bank on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held insecurely is not safely fixed or guarded, so it lacks any protection or security.

clue.text: Cashier sees tenpence stolen by slippery customer

indicators.note: money stolen by someone ends up held inside them, so the coins go within the eel

blocks.note: an eel is the proverbially slippery creature
X is the Roman numeral ten and P stands for pence

explanation.surface: A bank cashier watches a shifty customer pocket a ten-pence coin.
explanation.walkthrough: Cashier is not a bank clerk but the verb meaning to dismiss from service, especially from the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier someone is to throw them out of their post in disgrace, which is to remove or eject them.

clue.text: Part of central London toured by female engine driver?

indicators.note: a district toured by someone is surrounded by them as they go round it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: gal is an informal word for a girl or woman
Soho is a district in London's West End

explanation.surface: A woman train driver is shown round the West End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engine driver' suggests a train driver; here it is whatever drives an engine, a fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasohol is a petrol and alcohol fuel blend, so it is literally what powers or drives a motor.

clue.text: Slimy little thing being prodded by a pet

indicators.note: something prodded has another thing poked into it, so one piece is pushed inside the other

blocks.note: the Supreme Being is God
a pet is an old word for a fit of sulks, a strop

explanation.surface: A small slimy creature is poked by someone's pet animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Pet is not an animal but a sulk, as in 'in a pet'; a strop is British slang for a bad-tempered huff.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastropods are snails and slugs, small molluscs that leave a trail of slime.

clue.text: Draw, or do very badly?

blocks.note: first meaning: to pull in, as liquid through a straw
second meaning: a slang verb for being terrible at something

explanation.walkthrough: Draw suggests a tied match, set against doing badly; it is really the verb to pull in by mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to pull in with the mouth and, in slang, to be dreadful or perform poorly.

clue.text: Wave surfed finally with Charlie on the crest?

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word before it, so only its closing letter is used
to wave something is to shake it about, so these letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A surfer called Charlie rides the crest of a wave.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like the NATO alphabet's C, but the whole name is used. The crest is not a wave top but a coat-of-arms device.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is part of a coat of arms, so anything depicted on it belongs to the art of heraldry.

clue.text: The one remaining in a street after having left country

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street
Togo is a country in West Africa

explanation.surface: The last resident left on a street after everyone else has emigrated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places A ST after L; the country follows to give LAST TO GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever is the final person to leave is the one still there when all the others have departed.

clue.text: Those exchanged for chips, one swiped by gulls

indicators.note: something swiped by thieves ends up held in their grasp, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: to gull someone is to con them, a verb in the third person
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Seagulls snatch someone's chips at the seaside, after the money has been spent on them.
explanation.walkthrough: Gulls are not birds here but a verb meaning swindles. The chips are casino chips, not fried potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: At a casino, money in the form of cash is swapped for gaming tokens, and back again when you leave.

clue.text: See 26
Local distributor singing backwards – bewildering image?

indicators.note: going backwards means reading the word for singing from right to left

blocks.note: an optic is the measuring dispenser on an upside-down spirits bottle in a pub, and the local is one's nearby pub
tra-la is a burst of wordless singing

explanation.surface: A local supplier sings backwards, producing a confusing picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Local is British for the neighbourhood pub, not a nearby distributor; an optic doles out measures of spirits there.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is an abstract style built on illusions that dazzle and confuse the viewer's eye.

clue.text: Slam the 9, foolishly – into those?

indicators.note: acting foolishly means behaving in a muddled way, so these letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
the answer to 9 across

explanation.surface: A gambler foolishly slams their money into the fruit machines.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: coins are slammed into slot machines, foolishly, by gamblers at the seaside arcade.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaming machines operated by inserting money into a narrow opening are exactly what coins get fed into.

clue.text: Well, someone’s dog is barking, O no!

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go wild and come out in another order
'no' tells the solver that the round letter named just before it must be removed

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in dismay that their dog is barking.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one O from someone's dog, then rearrange. Barking means mad in British slang, not the dog's noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, used at the start of a remark like 'Well, I never'.

clue.text: 1 across activity where couple of fish sought, but something unpleasant netted?

indicators.note: something netted is caught inside, so it sits between the two fish

blocks.note: rock (rock salmon) is a fish sold in British chip shops; the first of the pair
a childish word for excrement
ling is a cod-like sea fish; the second of the pair

explanation.surface: A seaside pastime: hunting for fish but catching something nasty in the net.
explanation.walkthrough: The couple of fish are two separate fish names, with the unpleasant item caught between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Poking about in the pools among rocks on a beach for crabs and fish is a traditional activity at the coast.

clue.text: Meat joint guzzled by pop, nice one!

indicators.note: something guzzled is taken inside the drinker, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: pop is fizzy soft drink, such as cola
the hip is a joint of the body
ta is British informal thanks, which 'nice one!' expresses

explanation.surface: Dad scoffs a joint of meat and someone cheers him on.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop looks like father but is the fizzy drink. A chipolata is a small thin British sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipolata is a small sausage, so it is a piece of meat in the broad sense used in recipes.

clue.text: Similar-sounding donkey rides tiny animal

blocks.note: an ass is a donkey
one thing that rides another is on it
an ant is a tiny insect

explanation.surface: A donkey carries a tiny creature on its back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rides' supplies a little word for being on top, so the donkey sits on top of the insect in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Assonant describes words that echo each other in their vowel sounds, so they resemble one another to the ear.

clue.text: See 12 Across
Myopic Lilliputian watched

blocks.note: the Lilliputians in Gulliver's Travels are tiny people
to mind children is to watch over them

explanation.surface: A short-sighted tiny person being looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: Myopic is used figuratively here, of narrow outlook rather than poor eyesight.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative short-sightedness means a narrow, petty outlook that fails to look beyond the immediate.

clue.text: Body part in story on dance initially forgotten,

indicators.note: with its start forgotten, the word for the dance loses its opening letter

blocks.note: a fib is a small lie, a made-up story
the hula is a Hawaiian dance

explanation.surface: A tale about a dance whose start has slipped someone's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places the shortened dance after the story word, as in a down answer. The trailing comma is printed by the source.
explanation.definitionFit: The fibula is the thinner of the two lower leg bones, an anatomical piece of the human frame.

clue.text: Mole genitals discussed?

indicators.note: something discussed is talked about, so it is the spoken form of the word that counts

blocks.note: the groin is the area of the body around the genitals

explanation.walkthrough: Mole is not the animal or the skin blemish but a sea wall; a groyne is a barrier built out from a beach to stop erosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A mole is a breakwater or jetty of stone, and a groyne is a similar low wall running into the sea.

clue.text: US island has got it in the essence of tour

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
the essence of a thing is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the two middle letters of the word
'ah!' is what one says on getting it

explanation.surface: An American island has been grasped as the heart of a holiday tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got it' is an exclamation of understanding, not possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Oahu is the Hawaiian island that is home to Honolulu, part of the fiftieth US state.

clue.text: On pier, melt getting tanned in US state capital

indicators.note: to tan someone is to give them a beating, so these letters are knocked about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone melts in the sun on a seaside pier, getting a tan.
explanation.walkthrough: Tanned looks like suntanned, but it means beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Montpelier is the capital city of Vermont, one of the United States.

clue.text: Plant you recognised in France on border

blocks.note: tu is French for you
a lip is an edge or rim

explanation.surface: A plant spotted growing on a border while travelling in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Border suggests a flower bed, but it is an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: The tulip is a spring-flowering bulb grown in gardens, a familiar kind of flowering plant.

clue.text: Brobdingnagian kingdom, the bewitching peninsula finally found

indicators.note: what is found at the finish of each word is its closing letter, so those are kept

blocks.note: the last letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Gulliver's land of giants is an enchanting peninsula, at last discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: Brobdingnag is the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels, pairing with Lilliputian at 18 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything Brobdingnagian is gigantic, and mega is an informal word for huge or enormous.

clue.text: Room after musical for ‘70s rom-com

blocks.note: Annie is the musical about a little orphan
a hall is a large room

explanation.surface: A room comes after a musical, setting up a 1970s romantic comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the room after the musical in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Annie Hall is Woody Allen's 1977 romantic comedy film starring Diane Keaton.

clue.text: Those sold by the 1 across relished job on deck?

blocks.note: relish is a sauce, so something relished is sauced
a post is a position or job
a deck is a pack of playing cards

explanation.surface: A job on a ship's deck is something someone enjoys doing at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: Relished looks like enjoyed but means covered with relish. Saucy postcards are cheeky comic cards sold in British seaside resorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheeky, risqué picture cards are a staple souvenir sold in British coastal resorts.

clue.text: Sunburnt shoulders nursed by warty chap, a dish from Mexico?

indicators.note: shoulders are at the outer edges, so only the outside letters of the word are kept
something nursed is held in the arms, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a toad is a warty creature
the first and last letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone with sunburnt shoulders is cared for by an ugly man.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoulders is not a body part to treat but the two outer letters. The toad is a familiar warty creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A tostada is a crisp fried tortilla with toppings, a dish from Mexican cooking.

clue.text: Gentry, wrath in the gents, say?

blocks.note: what a man does in the gents, a British word for a men's toilet
rage is wrath, here imagined as rage while at the urinal, like road rage

explanation.surface: Someone is furious in the gentlemen's toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'wrath in the gents' as a jokey compound like road rage; the gents is British for a men's lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: The peerage is the nobility, the titled class, close to the landed gentry in a broad sense.
